newsitem.title: IRAQ: Sirens sound as U.S. missiles strike Iraq again.
newsitem.headline: Sirens sound as U.S. missiles strike Iraq again.

text.p: The United States launched a second wave of cruise missiles against Iraqi military targets in southern Iraq on Wednesday, pursuing its most serious military confrontation with President Saddam Hussein since the Gulf War.

U.S. officials said 17 missiles were fired from four ships in a "mop-up" operation authorised by President Bill Clinton. The second wave was aimed at military targets in southern Iraq not destroyed in an attack by 27 missiles on Tuesday.
They said the mission was intended to destroy Iraq's ability to attack aircraft enforcing an expanded no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
Saddam Hussein on Tuesday vowed to resist the U.S. attacks, launched in retaliation for Iraqi military intervention in the country's Kurdish north.
There was no official word in Iraq on Wednesday on the latest wave of cruise missiles.

In Baghdad, air raid sirens blared early in the morning while most of the four million residents were still asleep. There were few people on the streets, but none scrambled for cover or even bothered to stop and ask what the sirens were for.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Tuesday night that damage from the first wave of missiles had been "considerable". But he dismissed as "exceedingly unlikely" Iraqi reports that civilians were among the casualties, noting that the target sites were remote.
Perry said Iraq's military offensive against Kurdish rebels in the north posed a "clear and present danger" to neighbouring countries and the flow of oil.
Saddam reacted fiercely to the first wave of attacks, exhorting his forces to resist.

"You men of our air defence and falcons of the skies...Hit back with capability and efficiency, relying on God, the Almighty, at any hostile plane the aggressors fly to violate the airspace of your great country throughout Iraq," Saddam said on state television on Tuesday.
Iraq said minimal damage was done in the first attacks on Tuesday and that five people had been killed and 19 wounded. Some casualties were civilians, it said.

The United States has also hit at Iraq's already crippled economy, saying Baghdad would not be able to export oil for "some time", putting on hold a U.N. oil-for-food plan that would have allowed Iraqi crude onto the world market within weeks for the first time since the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Washington has received open support for its military attacks only from Britain and Germany.

China and Russia have urged restraint and France, throughout the past week, has been cautious. Some Arab countries condemned the cruise missile attacks. Key allies such as Saudi Arabia remained silent.
A divided U.N. Security Council is struggling with a response to the new Iraqi crisis, agreeing that Baghdad should withdraw its troops from the north but troubled by the U.S. intervention.
The United States used a 1991 Security Council resolution to justify its missile attacks on southern Iraq but it was questionable if the resolution in fact mandated such action.

The U.S. attacks on Tuesday sent oil prices soaring to post-Gulf War highs. By late on Tuesday markets had settled back but on Wednesday crude oil prices jumped again. In early Asian trading prices rose 30 cents a barrel, to $23.65 from $23.35 before news of the second strike.
In Iraq, the first attack and fading prospect of oil exports sent the dinar plummeting to 1,750 from 1,250 dinars to the dollar before recovering to 1,500.
Allied air and naval forces have kept Iraq under surveillance since the 1991 Gulf War to oust Iraq from Kuwait.

U.S. British and French warplanes police no-fly zones north of the 36th parallel in northern Iraq, to protect Iraq's Kurdish minority, and south of the 32nd parallel in southern Iraq to give similar haven to Shiite Moslems.
Clinton said the United States would expand the southern no-fly zone to the north by one degree of latitude to further reduce Iraq's room for manoeuvre toward Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

This will deny Saddam control of Iraqi air space from the Kuwaiti border to the southern suburbs of Baghdad," Clinton said in a statement from the White House. "It significantly restricts Iraq's ability to conduct offensive operations."
